title: Coding Agents for Teaching Economics
text:
Preface
This handbook is for people who teach economics and want to use a coding agent to prepare and run a module. It covers lecture material, problem sets and code labs, assessment design, marking, checking, and the rules that apply at UK universities.
The main text does not depend on a particular product. Notes headed In Claude Code give the specifics for that tool. Those notes, and the university policies cited, were checked on 26 and 27 November 2026 and will date.
The templates at the end of the handbook are also files in the templates/ folder of the repository. None has been tested on a live module.
The handbook gives general guidance, not legal advice. Your own institution’s policy takes precedence.
Licence. Text and templates are released under CC BY-NC 4.0: you may reuse and adapt them for non-commercial purposes with attribution.

title: 1  Scope and how to use this handbook
text:
This handbook is for colleagues who teach economics and want to use a coding agent to prepare and run a module. It covers lecture material, problem sets and code labs, assessment design, marking, checking, and the rules that apply.
A coding agent is a language model that reads the files in a folder on your computer, writes new ones and runs code. Chapter 2 explains how that differs from a chat window. No programming is needed to follow the handbook, although chapter 6 is most useful for modules with a computational component.
Tool. The main text does not depend on a particular product. Where the mechanics matter, a short note headed In Claude Code gives the specifics. Those notes were checked against the Claude Code documentation on 26 and 27 November 2026 and will date faster than the rest.
Examples. Most worked examples come from quantitative finance and econometrics. Each section also says how the same workflow applies to macroeconomics, applied economics and economic theory, where the material is more often derivations, models and essays than code.
Policy. Chapters 7, 8, 10 and 11 describe the position at UK universities in general. Your own institution’s policy takes precedence, and several of the rules differ across universities.
Out of scope. This is not a guide for students, and it does not cover research use. It does not compare products or discuss procurement.
Reading paths.

New to coding agents: chapters 2 to 4, then whichever of 5 to 8 matches the task in front of you.
Already using one: chapters 6 to 9, 12 and 14, and the templates.
Module or programme lead: chapters 7, 8, 10 and 11.
crumbs: 1  Scope and how to use this handbook

title: 2  What a coding agent is
text:
A coding agent works directly on the files in a folder, whereas a chat window works only on what is pasted or uploaded into the conversation. It is therefore more useful for preparing teaching material, and because it can change and delete files it needs closer supervision.









Chat window
Coding agent




What it sees
What you paste or upload
Every file in the folder you open it in


What it produces
Text in the conversation
Files on disk: notes, slides, notebooks, spreadsheets


Running code
Limited or none
Runs what is installed on your machine (Python, R, Stata, LaTeX) and reads the result


Continuity
Depends on what you re-supply or what the product remembers
Reads a standing instruction file at the start of every session


Scale
One document at a time
A whole module, or a folder of scripts, in one task



Products. Anthropic, OpenAI and Google each offer a coding agent alongside their chat products: Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI. The chapters that follow apply to all three. The notes headed In Claude Code give the specifics for one of them, and the other two have equivalent settings under different names.
In practice. You can ask for a problem set and its solutions, have the solutions executed, and get back the files with the numerical answers already checked. You can ask for the notation in ten weeks of slides to be made consistent. Neither is practical by copying and pasting.
Limits. The model still makes confident mistakes: a sign error in a derivation, a reference that does not exist, a question that is harder than intended. Running code catches numerical errors but not a wrong economic argument. Chapter 9 covers checking.
Permissions. Because the agent can edit and delete files, every product has a setting for what it may do without asking. For a first module:

Open the agent in a folder made for the module and never in your home folder.
Begin in the mode that asks before each edit, and relax it once you have seen how the agent behaves.
Keep the folder under version control (chapter 4), or at least in a synced drive with file history, so any change can be undone.


In Claude Code. It runs in a terminal, a desktop app, VS Code, JetBrains IDEs and the browser (platforms). The desktop app is the easiest start for colleagues who do not use a terminal.
The permission modes are Manual (asks before edits and commands), acceptEdits (edits files in the folder without asking), plan (reads and proposes, changes nothing until you approve) and auto (acts without asking, with a separate model reviewing its actions). Recent versions start interactive terminal and VS Code sessions in auto, so switch to Manual or plan for a first session. In the terminal, Shift+Tab cycles through the modes.
crumbs: 2  What a coding agent is

title: 3  Setting up a module folder
text:
Each module needs one folder, with your source material separated from what the agent produces and one short instruction file at the top. The chapters that follow assume this setup.
Folder layout. The layout below works for most modules.
ECN000-module-name/
  MODULE.md            standing instructions (see below)
  sources/             your notes, papers, past slides, textbook references (read-only)
  lectures/            week01/, week02/, ... notes and slides
  problem-sets/        ps1/ questions, solutions, code, data
  assessment/          coursework briefs, exams, rubrics, marking schemes
  data/                datasets used in labs and coursework
  admin/               module outline, schedule, announcements
Keep sources/ read-only by convention, so that the agent reads from it and never edits it. Keep assessment/ out of any folder that is shared with students or synced to the virtual learning environment.
The module instruction file. The agent reads this file at the start of every session, so it replaces the paragraph of context you would otherwise retype each time. It should hold:

Module facts: code, title, level, credits, cohort size, prerequisites.
Learning outcomes: as approved in the module specification.
What students already know: which mathematics, statistics and programming can be assumed, and what cannot.
Notation: your symbols for returns, expectations, estimators, vectors and matrices, and which textbook’s conventions you follow.
Software: language and version, permitted libraries, how code is run.
House style: slide template, length of a lecture, how worked examples are laid out, British spelling.
Rules: never invent a reference; never edit sources/; every numerical answer must come from code that has been run.
Decisions log: dated one-line notes on choices made, so they are not reopened next year.

Keep it to one or two pages, because a long file is followed less reliably than a short one, and put detail that applies to one task, such as a marking rubric, in its own file and point to it. A skeleton is template A.
Other fields. For a theory or macroeconomics module, the notation and assumed-mathematics entries matter most. For an applied or policy module, add the data sources you use and the standard of evidence you expect in written work.

In Claude Code. The instruction file is called CLAUDE.md and sits at the top of the folder. It is loaded at the start of every session, and the documentation recommends keeping it under 200 lines (memory). The /init command drafts one from the folder’s contents. A line such as @assessment/rubric.md imports another file.
Claude Code treats the file as context and does not enforce it, so the read-only convention for sources/ should also be set as a deny rule in the permission settings, and can be enforced with a hook (chapter 14). Claude Code also reads a file named AGENTS.md when no CLAUDE.md is present, which helps if colleagues use different tools. Separately, it keeps its own notes on your corrections (auto memory); review them occasionally.
crumbs: 3  Setting up a module folder

title: 4  Version control and GitHub
text:
An agent can change dozens of files in one task, so you need to see exactly what it changed and to be able to undo it. Version control records each change to the module folder as a dated step, and the agent can operate it for you. Git is the standard tool for this, and GitHub is the most widely used service for keeping a copy of the folder online.
Undo, review and record. Each saved step, called a commit, is a snapshot of the whole folder, so a task can be reversed in one step however many files it touched. The change view, or diff, shows the lines added and removed in each file. It is how you review an agent’s work before accepting it, and how you compare this year’s module with last year’s (chapter 5). Each commit also carries a dated message saying what changed and why, which complements the decisions log in the instruction file. File history on a synced drive restores one file at a time and shows neither the lines that changed nor which files changed together.

In Claude Code. Checkpoints let you rewind the agent’s edits within a session, but they track only changes made by its file-editing tools. A file changed by a command, such as a script that rewrites a dataset, is not tracked, and snapshots are kept for about 30 days. The documentation recommends Git for permanent history (checkpointing).

Vocabulary.








Term
Meaning
In a module




Repository
A folder whose history Git records
ECN000-module-name/


Commit
A saved state of the whole folder, with a message
“Week 5 notes: GMM example replaced”


Diff
The lines added and removed between two commits
The agent’s changes to the week 5 slides


Branch
A separate line of commits for trying something
A trial reordering of weeks 3 and 4


Remote
A copy of the repository elsewhere, usually on GitHub
The module’s private repository on GitHub


Push and pull
Sending commits to the remote, and fetching them from it
Updating GitHub after a day’s work


Pull request
A proposal to bring a branch into the main version, with its diff and comments
A teaching assistant’s corrections to problem set 3


.gitignore
A file listing what Git must never record
assessment/, licensed data



The agent does the typing. You do not need to learn Git commands, because the agent runs them when asked in plain words: “commit these changes with a message saying what changed”, “show me what changed in week 5 since last term”, “undo your last change”, “start a branch to try a new order for weeks 3 and 4”. Commit before and after each agent task, so that each task is one step in the history and can be undone on its own. Before a commit, ask the agent to list the files it includes, and check that none of them is material that must stay out of the repository. If you prefer not to use a terminal, the desktop app’s change view and GitHub Desktop show the same diffs.
Setting up.

Install Git. On a Mac it comes with Apple’s command-line tools (xcode-select --install); on Windows, install Git for Windows. GitHub Desktop is an optional program that does the same tasks through windows and buttons.
Ask IT first. Your university may already provide an approved GitHub organisation, which settles where the repository lives and who can see it.
Create a GitHub account if you need one. Staff at accredited institutions can apply for GitHub Education with an institutional email address and proof of employment. At the time of writing, verified teachers get a GitHub Team account and Copilot at no cost (GitHub Education).
Create one private repository per module, and sign in to GitHub on your own computer yourself. The agent should never handle your password or access tokens.
Make the first commit with the agent, after it has added the .gitignore file and shown you the list of files. Template N is a prompt for this step.

Material to keep out. Student work and marks, unreleased exam papers, licensed datasets and textbook material (chapter 10), and passwords or keys never go into a repository. A file deleted after it was committed remains in the history and in every copy anyone has made, and GitHub’s guidance says such data cannot be removed from other people’s copies (removing sensitive data). A password or key committed by mistake must be changed at once.
The .gitignore file keeps this material out automatically. The one in template M excludes assessment/, the third-party subfolder of sources/ and licensed data, so exam drafts need to be kept in whatever storage your university approves for them. A private repository is still held on GitHub’s servers, so the question in chapter 10 about approved tools applies to GitHub as well as to the agent.
Branches and pull requests. A branch is a trial version of the module. Restructure weeks 3 and 4 on a branch, compare the result with the main version, and keep or discard it; the main version is untouched until you decide. A pull request proposes bringing a branch into the main version and shows its diff, which you, a co-lecturer or a teaching assistant can comment on line by line before it is accepted. The independent review in chapter 9 then leaves a written record of what was checked and by whom.

In Claude Code. The desktop app shows the agent’s changes file by file and takes comments on individual lines, which the agent then acts on. It can also open a pull request from the session (desktop).

Issues as an errata list. An issue is a numbered note attached to the repository. Report each mistake in the material as an issue, and you or the agent can work through the list. A commit whose message says “Fixes #12” closes issue 12 when it reaches the main version, so the history shows when each error was reported and when it was corrected. In a private repository only invited collaborators can open issues, so students usually report mistakes through the virtual learning environment, and you copy each report in.
Publishing a module site. GitHub Pages publishes a website from a repository, as it publishes this handbook. On a free or Pro personal account it publishes only from public repositories, and publishing privately requires an organisation on GitHub Enterprise Cloud (GitHub’s plans). Keep the module repository private, publish released material from a separate public repository, and add each set of solutions to it only when the solutions are released.
Sharing. A department’s shared skills (chapter 13) are kept in a GitHub repository, and so is a plugin marketplace. A colleague can copy a repository and adapt it within the terms of its licence file. This handbook’s licence, CC BY-NC, allows non-commercial reuse with attribution.

title: 5  Lecture material from your own sources
text:
The agent is most reliable when it reorganises material you supply and least reliable when it writes from its own knowledge. Build lectures from your sources/ folder and treat anything it adds from outside as unverified.
Workflow.

Collect the sources. Put your notes, the papers and chapters the lecture draws on, and last year’s slides in sources/.
Ask for a plan before any writing. One page per lecture: the outcomes it serves, the sequence of ideas, the worked examples, what is cut. Edit the plan yourself to reflect what you know about the cohort.
Write the notes first. Full lecture notes in prose and mathematics, from the approved plan.
Derive the slides from the notes. The slides then follow the notes, and a later correction is made once, in the notes.
Generate every figure from code. Keep the script next to the figure so it can be rerun with new data.
Run a consistency pass. Across all weeks: notation, numbering, cross-references, terms defined before use.

File formats. Plain-text formats work best because the agent can compile them and compare versions: LaTeX and Beamer, or Markdown with Quarto. It can also produce PowerPoint and Word files, but changes are harder to review.
An example request.
Read sources/week05/ and the plan in lectures/week05/plan.md.
Write lecture notes for week 5 (generalised method of moments) in LaTeX.
Use only the material in sources/. Follow the notation in MODULE.md.
If you need a result that is not in the sources, stop and list it; do not supply it.
Aim for what can be taught in 100 minutes, with two worked examples.
Compile the file and fix any errors before you finish.
Common faults.

Length. Agents write too much. State the teaching time and the number of examples.
Level. The agent has no information about what your students find hard. Say so in the plan: where to slow down, which step needs intuition before algebra.
Invented support. References, dates, numbers in a motivating example and attributed quotations all need checking against a source (chapter 9).
Flat prose. Material written from generic knowledge reads like a textbook summary, whereas material built from your own notes keeps your examples and emphasis.

Updating a module year to year. Ask the agent to list what has dated: data ending in an old year, superseded references, examples overtaken by events. Rerun the figure scripts with current data. Review the changes in the change view against last year’s version before accepting them (chapter 4).
By field.

Econometrics and quantitative finance: have every estimate, table and figure in the notes produced by a script in the folder, on data students can also access.
Macroeconomics: model derivations benefit from the independent re-derivation in chapter 9. Charts of UK or international data should be built from the official series by script, with the download date recorded.
Economic theory: ask for proofs with every step written out, then have them checked separately. Agents skip steps that look obvious and are sometimes wrong.
Applied and policy modules: case studies are where invented facts appear most often. Supply the documents and require a citation for each factual claim.


In Claude Code. Use plan mode for step 2: the agent reads the sources and proposes, and nothing is written until you approve. Once the workflow is settled, store it as a skill so that a new lecture is one command (chapter 12).
crumbs: 5  Lecture material from your own sources

title: 6  Problem sets, solutions and code labs
text:
No solution goes to students unless it has been produced by code that ran, or re-derived independently. The rule is the main safeguard for exercises written by an agent, and an agent, unlike a chat window, can run the code itself.
Writing a problem set.

Specify before generating. The topic, the learning outcome each question tests, the number of questions, the intended time, and the mix of mechanical, applied and stretch questions.
Supply two or three of your own past questions as the standard for style and difficulty. Examples set the standard more reliably than a written description.
Ask for questions and solutions as separate files, with the solution code in a third.
Have the solution code executed and the numbers in the written solutions taken from its output rather than typed by the model.
Have the questions solved again from scratch by a separate session that has not seen the solutions, and compare (chapter 9 and template D).
Attempt the stretch questions yourself. Agents often misjudge how hard a question is.

Example: an empirical finance question. Students estimate the CAPM beta of five stocks on monthly returns and test whether the alphas are jointly zero. The agent writes the question, a script that downloads or loads the data and runs the regressions, and a solution whose betas, standard errors and test statistic are read from the script’s output. If the data file changes next year, rerunning the script updates the solution.
Variants. Once a question is driven by a script, a variant needs only a new seed, sample period or set of parameter values, and a rerun. Variants are useful for tutorial groups, resits and individualised coursework. Keep the seed and parameters for each variant in a file so any version can be reproduced.
Code labs and notebooks.

Require that each notebook runs from top to bottom in a clean environment before it is released. Ask the agent to do exactly that and report failures.
Pin the software: language version and package versions in a file in the folder.
Produce the student version from the solution version by removing marked cells, so the two cannot drift apart.
Keep data small and included in the folder, or downloaded by a script with the date recorded.

Software other than Python. The rule that numbers come from code that ran applies to any language the module uses. An agent can write a MATLAB, Stata or R script and run it from the command line, as long as the software is installed on the same computer and its licence covers that use: MATLAB through matlab -batch, Stata in batch mode, R through Rscript. The agent then reads the output as it would for Python. Some vendors also provide a connector that gives the agent more direct access to their software. Connectors use the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for linking an agent to other programs and services, and chapter 10 covers what to check before using one.

In Claude Code. MathWorks publishes an official MATLAB MCP Server. It lets the agent start MATLAB, run code, scripts and unit tests, and check a script for style and errors without running it. It needs MATLAB R2021a or later installed on your computer, and is added with claude mcp add --transport stdio matlab -- /fullpath/to/matlab-mcp-server-binary. According to its documentation, the server sends anonymised usage data to MathWorks unless it is started with --disable-telemetry=true, and under the MathWorks licence a server must not be shared by several users, so each lecturer or teaching assistant runs their own.

Questions without code.

Derivations and proofs (theory, macro): the equivalent of running the code is a symbolic or numerical check. Ask the agent to verify a closed-form answer with a computer algebra system, or to confirm a comparative-statics sign numerically at several parameter values. Such a check catches algebra slips but not flawed arguments.
Short-answer and essay questions (applied, policy): ask for a marking scheme alongside each question, stating what a pass, merit and distinction answer contains. Writing the scheme exposes questions that are vague or have several defensible answers.

Common faults.

Questions that are answerable without the intended method.
Numbers chosen so that the answer is uninformative, such as a test statistic nowhere near the critical value.
Solutions that state a correct number with an incorrect interpretation.
Questions that closely reproduce a textbook exercise (chapter 10).


In Claude Code. The agent runs the scripts and notebooks itself and reads the output, so step 4 is one instruction: “take every number in the solutions from the script output”. For step 5, a subagent starts with a fresh context and can be instructed to read only the questions (subagents). Template B stores steps 1 to 5 as a skill (chapter 12), using the checker in template D for step 5, and lists the stretch questions for step 6.
crumbs: 6  Problem sets, solutions and code labs

title: 7  Assessment design when students have the same tools
text:
Before setting any unsupervised assessment, give it to an agent yourself and mark what comes back. The marks show which parts of the assessment an agent cannot complete well, and so what the assessment still measures.
The stress test.

Start a fresh session in an empty folder, with none of your module files.
Give the agent exactly what a student receives: the brief, the data, the reading list.
Ask it to complete the assessment in one pass, then once more with one round of the kind of follow-up a student would give (“make it more critical”, “check the code runs”).
Mark both outputs against your rubric, ideally mixed in with past student scripts and marked blind.
Record where it lost marks, since those parts of the assessment still discriminate.

Template F turns these steps into a checklist. Repeat the test each year, because the tools improve and a result from two years ago says little about this year’s cohort.
Decide what must be shown unaided. Go through the learning outcomes and sort them into two groups: those a student must demonstrate without assistance, and those where using the tools well is part of the skill. The first group needs supervised conditions. The second can be assessed in coursework where AI use is permitted and the standard is raised accordingly.
Formats and what they still tell you.








Format
What it shows
Main cost




Invigilated written exam
Unaided knowledge and reasoning
Narrow range of skills; exam logistics


Invigilated computer exam, no network
Unaided coding and data work
Lab capacity; technical setup


Coursework plus short oral examination
Whether the student understands what they submitted
Staff time per student


Coursework with process evidence (drafts, version history, a log of AI use)
How the work was produced
Marking load; evidence can be manufactured


Coursework with AI permitted and assessed
Judgement: framing, verification, critique of output
Needs a rubric that rewards those things


In-class tasks and presentations
Performance in real time
Timetabling; anxiety for some students



Individualised data or parameters (chapter 6) deter copying between students but do not make a task harder for an agent.
State the rule for each assessment. Students need to know, per assessment, what use is allowed. A published scale helps keep this consistent across a programme. The AI Assessment Scale of Perkins, Roe and Furze is one such scale, with five levels running from “No AI” to “AI Exploration”.
Sector position. The Russell Group principles commit member universities to adapting teaching and assessment, upholding academic integrity, and attempting fair access where tools sit behind a paywall. If an assessment permits or expects AI use, check that every student can use an adequate tool at no cost.
Detection software. UCL states that it is not investing in detection software and that staff must not submit student work to such tools.
Lead times. Changing the assessment type or weighting can require a module amendment, which at some universities must be approved months ahead. A stress test in the spring leaves time to change the following year’s assessment.
By field. Take-home problem sets and empirical projects with a standard dataset are the most exposed. Proof-based theory questions and essays on well-covered topics should not be assumed safe; test them the same way. Work that depends on material the agent cannot see, such as an in-class experiment, a local dataset the student collected or a seminar discussion, is less so.
crumbs: 7  Assessment design when students have the same tools

title: 8  Marking and feedback
text:
The lecturer reads the work and sets the mark; the agent can help with everything around that. The university guidance cited below takes this position, and the evidence on machine marking supports it. Check your own institution’s rule before uploading any student work to any tool (chapter 10).
Evidence. Two recent UK studies of extended written work find that language models compress marks towards the middle.

Kay, Rutherford, Smith, Shore and Francis (2026), in Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, find that language models gave higher marks than human markers with much less spread, marking weak essays up and strong essays down.
Corsi et al. (2026) compare three models on 761 undergraduate psychology assignments from three UK universities. Agreement with human marks varied widely by model, prompt and institution, all models pulled marks towards the middle, and averaging across models did not remove the problem.

If compression towards the middle carries over to UK degree marking, the scripts most at risk are the fails and the firsts. Results are better for short structured answers. A study of an introductory programming course reports exact agreement between a model and human graders on 80% of 6,345 answers. None of these studies covers economics or finance.
University rules. Rules differ between universities, but the published guidance agrees on the points below.



Rule
Example




A human allocates the mark
York: marking is not delegated to AI, except questions with no academic judgement such as multiple choice


A subject expert reads every script
Exeter (September 2026)


Student work goes only into approved tools, or not at all
York requires explicit student permission; Exeter restricts it to licensed tools and requires students’ informed consent


Students are told when and how AI is used
York, Exeter


All markers on an assessment use the same approach
York, Exeter



A Loughborough review of staff guidance at 16 UK universities found that only a minority gave concrete direction on marking, moderation or feedback. If yours is silent, ask before proceeding.
Uses that stay inside these rules.

Rubric design. Draft and test a rubric against the learning outcomes before the assessment is set. No student work is involved.
Marking schemes for numerical work. Generate the scheme from the solution script, with method marks and common wrong answers.
Feedback from your notes. You read the script and write brief notes; the agent expands them into full sentences mapped to the rubric criteria. A prompt for this step is template C. You approve the result.
Cohort-level feedback. Summarise the themes in your own comments across all scripts into a report for the class.
Automated checks on code. Run each submission’s code against tests you wrote, as in conventional autograding; the agent helps write the tests.
Consistency checks. After marking, ask whether your comments and marks on a criterion are consistent across scripts. The agent sees your marks and comments, anonymised.

Uses to avoid.

Asking for a mark and adopting it.
Asking for a mark first and then reading the script. The suggested mark can anchor your judgement.
Uploading scripts with names or student numbers to a tool your university has not approved.
Sending feedback you have not read in full.

Where it is permitted and you want a second view. Mark first, record your mark, then compare. Treat a disagreement as a prompt to reread, in the same way as a second marker’s view, and keep the decision yours.

In Claude Code. Marking support works on files in a folder, so anonymise first: one file per script named by candidate number, with your notes alongside. Whether the tool may be used at all depends on the account type and your university’s approval (chapter 10).

title: 9  Checking the output
text:
Everything the agent produces is a draft until it has passed a check that does not rely on the session that wrote it. Students treat teaching material as correct, so an error in a solution or a slide costs more than an error in a draft paper.
Match the check to the kind of error.








Kind of error
Check
Who




Wrong number in a solution or table
Number is read from the output of code that ran
Agent


Code that fails on a student’s machine
Run from top to bottom in a clean environment with pinned versions
Agent


Algebra slip in a derivation
Symbolic or numerical verification of the result
Agent


Flawed step in a proof or argument
Independent re-derivation in a fresh session, then your own reading
Agent, then you


Reference that does not exist or does not say what is claimed
Each reference opened at its DOI or URL and the claim located in it
Agent, then you for key ones


Wrong fact, date or figure in an example
Traced to a document in sources/ or a cited official series
Agent


Inconsistent notation across weeks
Consistency pass against MODULE.md
Agent


Wrong level, emphasis or tone
Your reading
You



Fresh sessions. A session that has just written a solution may simply confirm it when asked to check. A second session that sees only the question has not seen the first answer. Where the two disagree, at least one is wrong, and the disagreement is where to look first.
An independent reviewer for all material. A second agent, not the one that wrote the material, should review every piece of it before the lecturer reads it, in three passes:

Correctness. Every statement, equation, number and reference is checked against the sources and the code output.
Typos and mechanics. Spelling, broken cross-references, mislabelled figures, equations that do not compile, slides that overflow.
Conformance to a written standard. The material is compared with a document that states how it should be written: the notation and house style in the instruction file, or a longer style guide stored as a skill (chapter 13 and template G). A guide to academic writing style, applied to papers and slides, is one example.

The third pass needs a written standard, such as a page of explicit rules. An instruction like “make it sound like me” gives the reviewer nothing to check against.
Keep the passes separate and ask for a list of findings with locations rather than a corrected file. You then decide which findings to accept, and the writing agent applies them. The review can catch errors before your own reading but does not replace it.
Independent re-derivation in practice.

Session A writes questions and solutions.
Session B receives the questions only and writes its own solutions.
A script or a third session compares the two and lists every disagreement.
You resolve the disagreements. Agreement does not prove correctness, because both sessions can share a misconception.

References. Require a DOI or stable URL for every reference in material the agent writes, and have each one opened and checked. Do not accept a reference the agent cannot open. For the handful of papers a lecture rests on, check them yourself.
Your own reading. Only you can judge whether an explanation is pitched at the right level, whether an example is fair to all students, and whether an argument is the one you want to teach. Read everything that goes to students at least once in full.
Before release.

Every number traced to code output
Code and notebooks run clean from top to bottom
Derivations and proofs independently re-derived
Every reference opened and confirmed
Notation checked against the instruction file
Independent review done: correctness, typos, conformance to the written standard
Read in full by the lecturer


In Claude Code. A subagent runs in its own context window and can be limited to read-only tools, which makes it a natural session B. Store it as a file in .claude/agents/ so the same checker is used every time (template D).

title: 10  Student data, copyright and institutional policy
text:
You may use your own teaching material with these tools. Student work and third-party material carry most of the risk, and your university sets the rules for both. This chapter is general guidance and not legal advice.
Kinds of material.








Material
Examples
Default position




Your own
Your notes, slides, questions, code
Free to use, subject to your employer’s IP policy


Student
Scripts, coursework, marks, emails, extenuating circumstances
Approved tools only, anonymised, and often not at all


Third party
Textbook chapters, publisher slides and test banks, journal articles, licensed datasets
Depends on the licence; ask the library



Student data. A script with a name or student number on it is personal data, and your university is responsible for how it is processed. Published UK policies are consistent on the default:

Liverpool lists uploading student work or personal data to public AI platforms as unacceptable without a data protection impact assessment or advice from the Data Protection Officer.
York requires explicit student permission before student work or details go into a generative AI tool.
Exeter notes that student work is by default the student’s intellectual property.

Anonymising helps, but an essay can still identify its author through its content, and the work still belongs to the student.
Approved tools and account types. Universities approve specific tools under specific contracts. A personal subscription to the same product is a different legal arrangement. The distinction that usually matters is whether the provider may train on what you send and how long it is kept.

In Claude Code. The data usage page distinguishes two cases. On personal plans (Free, Pro, Max, Ultra), data is used to train models when the account’s setting allows it, with retention of five years if allowed and 30 days if not. Under commercial terms (Team, Enterprise, API), prompts and code are not used for training unless the customer opts in, and standard retention is 30 days.
Session transcripts are also stored on your own machine, unencrypted, for 30 days by default, and transcripts of sessions started in the desktop app are kept with no age limit unless you set one. On a shared or unencrypted laptop, that is a further copy of anything you worked on.

Connectors. A connector links the agent to another program or service, such as a cloud drive, a data provider or a statistical package (chapter 6). Anything the agent reads or sends through a connector falls under the same rules as the rest of this chapter, and a connector to an external service is one more place where student work or licensed data can end up. Before using a connector in a folder that holds student work or licensed material, check what it reads and sends, and to whom. Your university’s approval of the agent may not cover the services its connectors reach.

In Claude Code. Connectors are MCP servers. The documentation advises verifying that you trust each server before connecting it, because a server that fetches external content can expose the agent to prompt injection: instructions hidden in that content which the agent may follow. Even a connector that runs on your own computer, such as the MATLAB server, may send usage data to its developer.

Third-party teaching material. Putting a textbook chapter or a publisher’s test bank into a prompt is likely to count as copying for copyright purposes. Whether it is licensed depends on your university’s agreements.

The Copyright Licensing Agency added permission for copying into generative AI prompts to its business licences in May 2025. For the Higher Education licence, publishers were consulted in summer 2026 on adding equivalent permissions. Whether these are now in force was not confirmed at the time of writing, so ask your library.
Where such permissions exist in other CLA licences, they exclude training and require a tool whose terms do not allow training on prompts. A personal account with training switched on would not qualify.
Licensed datasets used in teaching have their own terms. Check before placing them in a folder the agent reads.

Output that reproduces a source. An exercise that closely follows a textbook problem may still infringe the publisher’s copyright, however it was produced. Ask the agent to write new questions to your specification, and do not ask it to rephrase existing ones.
Practical rules.

Keep student work out of the module folder unless you are using an approved tool for an approved purpose.
Keep third-party material in a separate subfolder of sources/ so it is easy to exclude.
Find your university’s list of approved AI tools and its staff guidance before the first use, and reread it each year.
If the guidance is silent on what you want to do, ask your Director of Education or the data protection team, and keep the answer.
crumbs: 10  Student data, copyright and institutional policy

title: 11  What to tell students
text:
Put a short AI statement in the module outline that says what students may do in each assessment and what you did in preparing the module. Permitted use differs across modules and assessments, so students need the rule for yours in writing.
Contents.

Per assessment: what use is permitted, in concrete terms. “You may use AI to debug code but not to write the interpretation” can be applied; “Use AI responsibly” is too vague to apply.
Disclosure: what students must declare and where, for example a short paragraph at the end of the submission naming the tool and what it was used for.
Responsibility: the student answers for everything submitted, including errors and invented references introduced by a tool.
Access: which tool the university provides at no cost, so that no assessment depends on a paid subscription.
Verification: that you may ask any student to explain their submission in person.
Your own use: how AI was used in preparing materials and, if at all, in marking and feedback.

Disclosing your own use. Guidance at several universities, including York and Exeter, asks staff to tell students when and how AI is used in marking and feedback. Extending it to teaching materials takes one sentence and makes it easier to ask students for the same openness.
Teach the checking as well as the rule. The first two Russell Group principles are about AI literacy and about equipping staff to support students’ use of AI. In a quantitative module, the most useful habit to teach is the rule from chapter 6 that a number is not trusted until the code that produced it has run. A short in-class demonstration of an agent producing a plausible but wrong answer makes the point concretely.
Keep it consistent across the programme. Agree a common format with colleagues so students see the same structure in every module, even where the permitted use differs. A shared scale (chapter 7) is one way to do this.
A model statement to adapt is template E.

title: 12  Writing skills
text:
A skill is a task you have done well once, written down so that the agent does it the same way every time. A tested skill can be reused for years and handed to a colleague.
Where instructions go. The handbook uses four places for instructions.











Instruction file
Prompt
Skill
Subagent




Holds
Facts and rules for every task in the module
A one-off request
The procedure for one recurring task
A role that needs its own context


Read
At the start of every session
When typed
When called, or when the task matches its description
When called


Example
Notation; “never edit sources/”
“Cut the week 5 slides to 20”
A new problem set
The checker; the candidate


Chapter
3
5
This one
9, 15



Rules that apply to every task go in the instruction file, and a request you have typed twice should become a skill. A role that must not see what the main session has seen needs a subagent.
When a task is worth a skill. A task is worth a skill when it recurs, weekly, annually or across the modules of a programme, when you can state the right way to do it, including the checks, and when a mistake costs enough that you want the checks applied every time. The clearest signal is that you have typed much the same request twice, or corrected the agent in the same way twice. A task done once is not worth a skill, and neither is one where judgement is the whole task, such as setting a mark.
What a skill contains. Write it as you would brief a capable teaching assistant who has never seen the module. Template B, the problem-set skill, has each part.

Description. One or two sentences on what the skill does and when to use it. It matters most, because the agent reads only the descriptions until a skill is needed and chooses from them. Put the main use first, in the words a colleague would use to ask for it.
Inputs. Which files it needs, where they are, and what to do if one is missing. “Stop and list what is missing” is usually right.
Steps. In order, with the checks from chapter 9 included as steps.
Output. Which files, where, and a closing report: what was produced, what was verified and how, and what could not be verified.
Prohibitions. What the agent must not do.
Supporting files. Rubrics, past questions, longer examples and scripts, kept in the skill’s folder and read only when the main file points to them. The main file stays short and the detail is there when needed. Template G keeps its examples this way.

Facts about one module, such as its notation, software and file names, belong in the instruction file. A skill that contains them works only in the module it was written for. A skeleton is template I.

In Claude Code. A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file, in .claude/skills/<name>/ inside the module folder, or in ~/.claude/skills/<name>/ for use across all your modules. If both hold a skill with the same name, the personal one is used (skills).
The file opens with a short header of settings. description is the only one the documentation recommends. disable-model-invocation: true means the skill runs only when you type its name, which suits a skill that edits many files or runs for a long time; template H uses it. argument-hint shows what to type after the name, and allowed-tools lets the skill use named tools without asking. The documentation advises keeping SKILL.md under 500 lines, and descriptions longer than 1,536 characters are cut short in the list the agent reads. Edits to a skill take effect without restarting.

Put the fixed steps in a script. Some steps have only one correct outcome: compiling a document, running a notebook from top to bottom, producing the student version of a notebook by removing the solution cells, confirming that each DOI resolves, checking a closed-form result symbolically. For these steps, put a script in the skill’s folder and have the skill run it. The script then does the parts where only one answer is acceptable, as chapter 6 requires for numbers, and the agent handles the judgement around it. Template K bundles a script that releases a notebook.

In Claude Code. Scripts in the skill’s folder are run, not read into the conversation, and ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR} in SKILL.md stands for that folder’s path. allowed-tools can let one script run without a permission prompt, for example Bash(${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/release.py *). A line written as !`command` runs when the skill is called, and its output replaces the line before the agent reads it, which is one way to supply the current date or the list of weeks.

From a typed request to a shared skill. A skill such as template B usually develops from a request typed by hand.

A request typed three times. In weeks 3, 5 and 8 the lecturer asks for a problem set, each time in slightly different words. The week 8 request leaves out “take every number from the script output”, and one solution contains a number the model typed.
A first skill. The week 5 request, the best of the three, is saved as a file. Weeks 9 and 10 come out without the omission.
A failure elsewhere. A colleague runs the skill on a macroeconomics module whose problem sets are derivations. It still asks for generalised method of moments, the Fama-French factors and the week 5 notation, because those were in the request it was saved from, and it has no step that checks a derivation.
A revised skill. The topic now arrives with the command (/problem-set week07), and notation comes from each module’s instruction file. Final expressions are verified symbolically or numerically, and the independent re-solve from chapter 6 is handed to the checker subagent (template D). The skill gains test cases and an owner, and is shared.

Stage 4 is template B. Compared with the request in stage 1, it includes the checks as steps, so they cannot be forgotten, and it leaves what is specific to one module to that module’s instruction file.
Testing a skill. A skill produces material students rely on, so test whether it starts when it should, and only then, and whether its output passes the checks.

Test cases. Keep three to five inputs, each with a short list of what a correct output must contain, such as “every number in the solutions appears in the script output” or “the report lists the stretch questions”. Template L gives the format. Store them in the skill’s folder without pointing to them from the main file, so they are not read in normal use.
The trigger. Write five requests a colleague might make for the task and five for neighbouring tasks, and see which ones start the skill. If the wrong ones do, make the description more specific.
A comparison without the skill. Run the same request with and without the skill, each in a fresh session. If the output is no better with it, drop the skill.
Someone else’s module. Run it on a module other than the one it was written for. If it works only on yours, the module-specific parts belong in the instruction file.

Rerun the test cases after every edit and after each update to the tool or the model, since an update can change how a skill behaves.
Maintaining a skill.

End the file with an owner, the date it was last tested and a short change log.
When you correct the agent’s output in the same way twice, add the correction to the skill as a rule. Chapter 13 applies the same rule to a written style standard.
Archive a skill nobody has used for a year, so that it does not mislead a successor.
Keep skills free of student data and assessment content, because anything in a skill is shared with it.

Skills from other people. A skill can run scripts on your computer with your permissions. Read a skill and its scripts before you use it, as you would code from a colleague. That includes the skills in a module folder you inherit.

In Claude Code. The documentation warns that a skill can grant itself broad tool access, and advises reviewing the allowed-tools of skills in a repository before running Claude Code there (skills).

By field.

Econometrics and quantitative finance: releasing a notebook (template K), and generating variants of a question from a file of seeds and parameters (chapter 6).
Macroeconomics: updating data, with official series downloaded by script and the download date recorded. Template J covers the annual update of a whole module.
Economic theory: a derivation check that bundles a script for symbolic verification, so the same check runs on every proof-based problem set.
Applied and policy modules: a citation check that opens each source cited in a case study and finds the claim in it.

title: 13  Sharing skills across a teaching team
text:
Once a task works well in one module, write it down as a skill (chapter 12) and share it. A department then needs each procedure to be worked out only once for all its lecturers.
Items to share.








Item
What it is
Who benefits




Module template
The empty folder layout and a skeleton instruction file (chapter 3)
Anyone starting or inheriting a module


Skills
Step-by-step instructions for a recurring task: new lecture, new problem set, annual update, stress test
Colleagues doing the same task


Checker
The independent checker from chapter 9, as a stored definition
Lecturers and teaching assistants


Statement template
The student-facing AI statement (chapter 11)
The whole programme



Chapter 12 covers how to write and test a skill. Before sharing one, run its test cases on a module other than the one it was written for.
Personal, module and department skills. Personal skills record how you work, such as your written standard below. Module skills hold the procedures for one module and live in its folder, so they pass to whoever teaches it next. Department skills hold what every module should do the same way: the checker, the stress test, the notebook release. Give department skills a common prefix so that they cannot be confused with a module’s own, and give each one an owner who reviews changes before they are shared.
Building a written standard for the reviewer. The third review pass in chapter 9 needs a document that says how your material should be written. It is built from your own work.

Collect examples. Five to ten pieces you consider your best: lecture notes, slides, problem sets, or papers if the standard is for research writing.
Have the agent extract the rules. Ask it to read them and list what is consistent: sentence and paragraph length, how a slide is structured, how a result is introduced, how equations are referenced, what is never done.
Edit the rules yourself. Delete what is accidental, correct what it misread, and add the rules you know you follow that the examples did not show.
Add pairs of examples. For each important rule, one passage that breaks it and the corrected version. The pair gives the reviewer something concrete to match.
Add a list of what to flag. The phrases and constructions you do not want, including those typical of machine-written text.
Say how to report. Findings as a list with location, the rule broken and a suggested fix. No rewriting.
Test it on old material. Run the reviewer on something you wrote before the standard existed, and on something an agent wrote. Adjust rules that produce false alarms.
Keep it current. Each time you correct the agent’s writing by hand, ask whether the correction is a rule. If so, add it.

One to three pages is enough. A standard built this way is specific to its author, so share the method and the template with colleagues rather than your own rules. A skeleton is template G.
Where to keep shared files. Keep them in a departmental repository (chapter 4) or shared drive, with one owner per file, and keep that location free of student data and of assessment content: skills and templates only.
Teaching assistants. Give assistants the checker and the problem-set skill but not the assessment folder. Agree in advance what they may use an agent for, and apply the same rule to all assistants on a module.
Handing a module over. The instruction file with its decisions log, the figure and solution scripts, and the module’s skills together are the handover. A successor can ask the agent to explain how any week’s material was built and regenerate it.

In Claude Code. Module skills are committed with the module folder in .claude/skills/, and personal skills sit in ~/.claude/skills/ (chapter 12). The checker is a subagent definition in .claude/agents/. A department can package its skills and subagents as a plugin and list it in a marketplace, which is a Git repository containing a .claude-plugin/marketplace.json file. Colleagues add the marketplace with claude plugin marketplace add and install from it with claude plugin install. A plugin’s skills are called as /plugin-name:skill-name, so they cannot clash with a module’s own skills.
The documentation warns that an installed plugin can run arbitrary code with your user privileges, and advises reviewing a plugin before installing it, whichever marketplace it comes from (plugin security). Skills follow the open Agent Skills standard, so the same files are usable in other tools that support it.
crumbs: 13  Sharing skills across a teaching team

title: 14  Automation
text:
Once a module is on GitHub (chapter 4), checks and agents can run without you starting them. Each one runs on someone else’s servers, so the rules in chapter 10 apply, and each one uses time, money or a usage allowance.
Checks on every change. GitHub Actions runs the steps in a workflow file, kept in the repository’s .github/workflows/ folder, whenever the repository changes. For a module, the useful steps are the ones on the release checklist in chapter 9 that a machine can do: compiling every LaTeX file, and running every notebook from top to bottom in a clean environment. A failure is reported against the change that caused it, so a broken notebook is found on the day it breaks. Template O is a workflow for both checks.
Standard runners are free in public repositories. Private repositories get a monthly allowance expressed in money, $12 on the free plan and $18 on Pro, which at GitHub’s published Linux rate is roughly 2,000 and 3,000 minutes (Actions billing). Check the usage page after the first week of term to see how much of it the module’s checks take.
Rules the agent cannot skip. The instruction file states rules but does not enforce them (chapter 3). A hook is a short script that runs at a fixed point, for example just before the agent edits a file, and a hook that runs before an action can block it. Hooks suit rules that must hold every time, such as no edits to sources/, no file written that contains a student number, or a compile check after every edit to a .tex file. Template P blocks edits to sources/ and pairs the hook with a permission deny rule.
Neither a hook nor a deny rule stops every route to a file. A script the agent runs, such as a Python program that writes its output into the folder, is outside both. Where a folder must not change at all, make it read-only on your computer as well.

In Claude Code. A PreToolUse hook runs before a tool call and can block it, by exiting with code 2 or by returning a deny decision. A PostToolUse hook runs after the call and cannot undo it. Hooks are set in .claude/settings.json, which is committed with the module, in .claude/settings.local.json for yourself only, or in ~/.claude/settings.json for all your projects (hooks guide).
An Edit deny rule covers all the built-in tools that edit files. It also covers shell commands that Claude Code recognises, such as sed and output redirection, but not arbitrary scripts (permissions).

Agents started from GitHub. With an integration installed, a comment that mentions the agent in an issue or a pull request starts it on the repository, and it pushes its changes for review. An erratum reported as an issue (chapter 4) can then be fixed by the agent and checked by you before the change is accepted. The work runs on GitHub’s servers and uses both the Actions allowance and the agent’s own usage. Give the integration only the permissions it needs, and read every change before accepting it.

In Claude Code. The integration is installed with /install-github-app, which needs admin access to the repository and works only with repositories on github.com. It authenticates with an API key, or with a subscription token on Pro, Max, Ultra, Team and Enterprise plans. The documentation warns never to commit either to the repository (GitHub Actions).

Sessions that run while your computer is off. A cloud session works on a copy of the repository on the provider’s servers and pushes its changes to a branch for you to review. A scheduled task runs on a timetable, for example to refresh the data behind the figures every Monday or to check every reference link two weeks before term. Both need the module on GitHub. Both also send its contents to outside servers, so no repository they can read should contain student work.

In Claude Code. Cloud sessions need GitHub to copy the repository and open pull requests. They are available on Pro, Max, Ultra and Team plans, and on Enterprise with qualifying seats (on the web). Scheduled tasks are available on Pro, Max, Ultra, Team and Enterprise plans and put their changes on branches whose names begin claude/. They were described as a research preview when this chapter was written (scheduled tasks).

Deciding what to automate.

Automate checks freely, since they report and change nothing.
Automate changes only where each one arrives as a pull request that you review.
Never automate anything that reads or changes student work or marks.
Record each automation in the instruction file’s decisions log, with what triggers it and what it may change, so that a successor knows what runs.

By field. Modules built on data gain most from scheduled refreshes, and modules with many notebooks from checks on every change. For a theory module, compiling every document on each change is usually enough.

title: 15  From assistant to agent: a worked example
text:
An assessment can be tested by three agents, one that sets it, one that sits it and one that marks it, in a cycle that repeats until a stopping rule set in advance is met. It is the only system in the handbook in which the software decides its own next step.
Assistant or agent. In chapters 5 to 9 you set each task, approve the plan and fix the steps in advance. The work is therefore supervised. An agent in the stricter sense is given a goal and a stopping rule and chooses its own actions from what it observes. The stress test in chapter 7 is the manual version of this system.
Separate roles.









Role
Sees
Produces
Must not see




Setter
Learning outcomes, constraints, the examiner’s last report
The brief, data and rubric; a log of each change and its reason
The candidate’s working


Candidate
Only what a student receives
A complete submission
The rubric’s marking notes, the setter’s intentions, earlier rounds


Examiner
The submission and the rubric
A mark per criterion with a one-line justification
Who or what wrote the submission



The design depends on this separation, because a candidate that has seen the marking notes, or an examiner that knows the submission is machine-written, gives no information about the assessment.
One round.

The setter writes or revises the assessment and records what changed and why.
The candidate attempts it in a clean folder with only the student-facing files.
The examiner marks the attempt against the rubric, criterion by criterion.
The system checks the stopping rule.
If it is not met, the setter reads the examiner’s report, identifies the criteria the candidate passed most easily, and revises.




The assessment loop: three roles and one decision


Each pass runs left to right; an unmet stopping rule sends the examiner’s report back to the setter.
The stopping rule. Set it before the first round. For example: stop when the candidate’s mark falls below 50, or after five rounds, or when the setter cannot propose a change that respects the constraints. The third condition matters because some assessments cannot be made robust in their current format, and a report that says so is a useful result.
Constraints on the setter. Without them the loop converges on an assessment that defeats the candidate and is worthless for students. State them as rules the setter must satisfy in every round:

Every learning outcome assessed in the original is still assessed.
The format, weighting, word limit and time allowance are unchanged unless you allow otherwise.
A well-prepared student can complete it in the time given, using only what the module taught.
No change relies on obscurity, trick wording or information students cannot reasonably obtain.
Each change is logged with the criterion it targets.

The changes left open by these constraints mostly tie the task to something the candidate does not have: work done in class, data the student collects, a position defended orally, or a judgement that must be justified against material specific to the module.
The report. It gives the original and final versions side by side, the change log, the mark by criterion in every round, the final attempt in full, and the setter’s own assessment of which constraints came under strain.
The lecturer’s part.

Mark the final attempt yourself. The examiner is a language model, and chapter 8 documents how such marks are compressed towards the middle. Its marks steer the loop but are not evidence that the assessment is safe.
Judge validity. Read the final version as a student would, and check that it is still a valid test of the learning outcomes and not only a harder one.
Check the examiner once. Before trusting the loop, give the examiner two or three model answers you have written at known standards and see whether it ranks them correctly. Do not use real student scripts for this unless your university permits it (chapter 10).

Limits.

The candidate models a capable student using a current tool with little effort, which is the case the assessment has to withstand, and says nothing about how real students at different levels will perform.
The result is specific to the tool and the date. Record both and rerun each year.
A full run uses many times the computation of a single request. Start with a round limit of three.
This system has not been run on a live module. Treat the files in template H as a starting design.

Other uses of the same three roles. For an invigilated exam, where AI use is not the concern, the loop still improves quality, because the candidate reports ambiguous wording and questions it could not finish in the time, and the examiner reports where the marking scheme gave no guidance. The setter revises for clarity instead of robustness.
By field. For empirical coursework, give the candidate the dataset and let it run code. For a theory problem set, the examiner needs full worked solutions in addition to final answers. For essay-based modules, expect the examiner’s marks to be least reliable, and rely more on your own marking of the final attempt.

In Claude Code. The candidate and examiner are subagents, each a file in .claude/agents/ with its own instructions and tool list. Setting omitClaudeMd: true starts a subagent without the module instruction file, which the candidate needs. The main session plays the setter and runs the loop from a skill.
A subagent in the same folder can still open files it is told not to. For a stricter test, copy the student-facing files to an empty folder outside the module and run the candidate there.
crumbs: 15  From assistant to agent: a worked example

title: Templates
text:
The sixteen templates below are starting points to copy and edit. A, C, E, F, L, M and N work with any tool, and O works with any repository on GitHub. B, G and I are skills, stored as a SKILL.md file, a format that Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI all read, so they should need little change, except that B hands its checking step to the subagent in D. J and K are skills that also use Claude Code settings, such as disable-model-invocation, which other tools may not accept. D defines a subagent with Claude Code’s settings, such as the list of tools it may use, and H combines a skill with two such subagents; both need rewriting for another tool, as does the Claude Code hook in P. None has been tested on a live module, so run each on a small example first. Each is also a file in the templates/ folder of the repository.

A. Module instruction file
Save as MODULE.md, or under the name your agent reads at the start of every session: CLAUDE.md in Claude Code, AGENTS.md in Codex, GEMINI.md in Gemini CLI.
# ECN000 Module Title

## Module facts
Level 6, 15 credits, about 120 students. Prerequisites: ECN000, ECN000.

## Learning outcomes
1. ...
2. ...

## What students know
Assume: linear algebra to eigenvalues, OLS, basic Python (pandas, numpy).
Do not assume: maximum likelihood, matrix calculus, any R or Stata.

## Notation
Returns r_t, excess returns r^e_t. Vectors bold lower case, matrices bold upper case.
Estimators carry a hat. Follow the conventions of [textbook], chapters [x-y].

## Software
Python 3.12. Packages pinned in requirements.txt. No other packages.

## House style
British spelling. Lecture notes in LaTeX using lectures/template.tex.
One lecture is 100 minutes: at most 25 slides and two worked examples.

## Rules
- Never edit anything in sources/.
- Never supply a reference, fact or number that is not in sources/ or code output.
  If something is missing, stop and list it.
- Every number in a solution comes from a script that has been run.
- Compile or run every file before reporting it finished.
- No student work or personal data is stored in this folder.

## Decisions log
2026-11-26  Dropped the Kalman filter lecture; replaced by a second GMM lab.


B. Problem-set skill
Save as .claude/skills/problem-set/SKILL.md, with the checker from template D in .claude/agents/. Run with /problem-set week05.
---
name: problem-set
description: Draft a problem set with verified solutions for one week of the module.
---

Write a problem set for $ARGUMENTS.

1. Read CLAUDE.md, the lecture notes for that week, and two past problem sets
   in problem-sets/ as the standard for style and difficulty.
2. Propose a one-page plan: each question, the outcome it tests, the expected
   time, and whether it is mechanical, applied or stretch. Wait for approval.
3. Write questions.tex, solutions.tex and solve.py in a new folder.
4. Run solve.py. Take every number in solutions.tex from its output.
5. For derivations, verify each final expression symbolically or numerically.
6. Compile both .tex files and fix any errors.
7. Use the checker subagent on the new folder: it solves questions.tex
   without seeing solutions.tex, then compares. Do not change a solution
   to match the checker; list every disagreement for me to resolve.
8. Report: what was produced, what was verified and how, every disagreement
   the checker found, and anything you could not verify. List the stretch
   questions so that I can attempt them myself.

Do not reuse or paraphrase questions from textbooks in sources/.


C. Marking notes to feedback
Use only with a tool your university has approved for student work (chapter 10).
Below are my marking notes for one anonymised script and the rubric.
I have already set the mark; do not suggest or comment on a mark.

Write feedback of about 150 words:
- one sentence on what the script did well, taken from my notes;
- the two most important improvements, each tied to a rubric criterion;
- one concrete step for the next assessment.

Use only what is in my notes. Do not add observations of your own.

Rubric: [paste]
Notes: [paste]


D. Independent checker
Save as .claude/agents/checker.md.
---
name: checker
description: Independently solves a problem set from the questions alone and reports disagreements with the official solutions. Use before any solutions are released.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---

You are checking a problem set for a university module.

1. Read the questions file only. Do not open the solutions yet.
2. Solve every question yourself. You cannot run code: where a number requires
   computation, write the code in your report and mark the number as unconfirmed.
3. Only then read the official solutions.
4. For each question report: agree, or disagree with both answers and the
   likely source of the difference.
5. Separately list any question that is ambiguous, answerable without the

name: lecture-style
description: House style for lecture notes and slides in my modules. Use when writing or reviewing any teaching material.
---

## Rules
1. One idea per slide. A slide has a title that states the point, not the topic.
2. Paragraphs in notes are at most four sentences.
3. Every equation that is used later is numbered; no others are.
4. A new symbol is defined in the sentence where it first appears.
5. Each result is followed by one sentence of interpretation in plain words.
6. Worked examples use real data and state the source and sample period.

## Do not
- Open a section by announcing what it will do.
- Use rhetorical questions as slide titles.
- Use: "it is important to note", "delve", "crucial", "in today's world".

Breaks rule 1:   title "Fama-MacBeth regressions"
Corrected:       title "Fama-MacBeth: estimate the price of risk period by period"
(more pairs in examples.md)

## When reviewing
Do not rewrite. Report each finding as:
  file and location | rule number | what is wrong | suggested fix
Finish with a count of findings per rule.

O. Checks on every change
The GitHub Actions workflow from chapter 14. It compiles every LaTeX document and runs every notebook in lectures/ and problem-sets/, and needs a requirements.txt listing the module’s Python packages. Save as .github/workflows/module-checks.yml.
# Save as .github/workflows/module-checks.yml in the module repository.
# On every push to main and every pull request, it compiles each LaTeX file
# that contains \documentclass and runs each notebook from top to bottom,
# in lectures/ and problem-sets/. Untested on a live module. If GitHub
# reports an action version below as out of date, update it.
name: Module checks

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  latex:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install LaTeX
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
            texlive-latex-recommended texlive-latex-extra \
            texlive-fonts-recommended latexmk
      - name: Compile every document
        run: |
          status=0
          while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
            grep -q '\\documentclass' "$f" || continue
            echo "::group::$f"
            if ! (cd "$(dirname "$f")" && latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error "$(basename "$f")"); then
              echo "::error file=$f::did not compile"
              status=1
            fi
            echo "::endgroup::"
          done < <(find lectures problem-sets -name '*.tex' -print0 2>/dev/null)
          exit $status

  notebooks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - name: Install the pinned packages
        run: |
          if [ -f requirements.txt ]; then pip install -r requirements.txt; fi
          pip install nbconvert ipykernel
      - name: Run every notebook from top to bottom
        run: |
          status=0
          while IFS= read -r -d '' nb; do
            echo "::group::$nb"
            if ! jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute --output-dir "$RUNNER_TEMP/executed" "$nb"; then
              echo "::error file=$nb::did not run"
              status=1
            fi
            echo "::endgroup::"
          done < <(find lectures problem-sets -name '*.ipynb' -not -name '*-student.ipynb' -not -path '*/.ipynb_checkpoints/*' -print0 2>/dev/null)
          exit $status


P. A hook that protects sources/
The hook from chapter 14, for Claude Code. Save the script as .claude/hooks/protect-sources.py (it is in the repository’s templates/ folder), and add the settings below to .claude/settings.json. The deny rule covers the editing tools and the shell commands Claude Code recognises, and the hook gives the agent a clear reason when it blocks an edit. Neither stops a script the agent runs from writing into the folder, so make sources/ read-only on your computer as well.
{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": ["Edit(/sources/**)"]
  },
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write|NotebookEdit",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "python3 \"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/protect-sources.py"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
